Lats Exercises

The lats are the large, wing-shaped muscles on each side of your back. They create much of the width of the upper body and do most of the work when you pull your arms down from overhead, as in pull-ups and lat pulldowns.

📍 The sides of the back, running from the mid-spine and pelvis up to the upper arm 10–20 sets/week

Anatomy

The latissimus dorsi originates from the lower thoracic and lumbar spine, the pelvis and the lower ribs, and inserts on the front of the upper arm bone (humerus). Because it attaches to the arm, it moves the shoulder when it contracts — drawing the arm down and back toward the torso.

Function

Shoulder extension and adduction — pulling the arm down and back; assists in spinal stability

Min Sets/Week
10
Optimal Range
10–20
Max Sets/Week
20

  • Straight-Arm Pulldown
  • Cable Pullover
  • Machine Pullover

Training Tips

  • Think of driving your elbows down toward your hips rather than pulling with your hands.
  • Get a full stretch at the top of every pulling rep, then finish with the shoulder blades down.
  • Mix vertical pulls (pulldowns, pull-ups) with rows so you train both width and thickness.

Where lats fits in a workout split

You can train lats in a push pull legs, upper/lower split or the bro split. Not sure which suits your schedule? Use the Split Finder, or see how weekly sets stack up in the workout planner.

FAQ

How often should I train lats?▾
Most people benefit from training lats 2 times per week. This provides enough frequency for muscle protein synthesis while allowing adequate recovery between sessions.
How many sets per week for lats?▾
10–20 working sets per week is a reasonable range for most trainees. Start at the lower end and increase gradually as your recovery allows.
What is the best exercise for lats?▾
The best exercise depends on your equipment and goals. For overall development, pull up is typically one of the most effective choices.
